a: to Ithiel, to Ithiel and Ucal:
p: The same Hebrew letters can be read as two names or as a cry: "I am weary, God... and worn out."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), as the Masoretes vowelled it; KJV and some modern versions
readings.en: to Ithiel, to Ithiel and Ucal
readings.plain: to Ithiel, to Ithiel and Ucal:

readings.w: Same consonants with other vowels (la'iti 'el... wa'ekhel), a proposal of modern scholars followed in many modern versions
readings.en: I am weary, God, I am weary, God, and I am spent
readings.plain: "I am weary, God, I am weary, God, and I am worn out."

readings.orig: τάδε λέγει ὁ ἀνὴρ τοῖς πιστεύουσιν θεῷ, καὶ παύομαι
readings.en: this is what the man says to those who trust in God, and I stop
readings.plain: to those who trust in God, and I stop:

readings.orig: vir cum quo est Deus et qui Deo secum morante confortatus ait
readings.en: the man with whom God is, and who, strengthened by God staying with him, said
readings.plain: the man with whom God is, and who is strengthened by God:

why: The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew as it has been read for a thousand years. But the vowels were added long after the letters, and many scholars think the cry "I am weary, God" fits Agur's confession in 30:2–3 better. The repeated name would be odd, and the Greek and Latin both saw words here, not names, though each read different words. The case is open.
b: The Greek also turns Agur's own name and his father's into words: "Fear my words, son, and receive them and repent." Jerome's Latin translates the names: "The words of the Gatherer, son of the Vomiter" (verba Congregantis filii Vomentis), the same wordplay found in the rabbis (Kohelet Rabbah 1:1). Some modern scholars read lo' 'iti 'el, "there is no God with me", or similar, as a skeptic's opening; this is a more radical change.

t: "I have not learned" or "God has taught me"?
p: The Greek turns Agur's confession around: "God has taught me wisdom."

readings.en: and I have not learned wisdom

readings.orig: θεὸς δεδίδαχέν με σοφίαν, καὶ γνῶσιν ἁγίων ἔγνωκα
readings.en: God has taught me wisdom, and I know the knowledge of holy ones

why: The Hebrew is clear, and the Greek translator seems to have softened a confession that sounded too bleak for a sage. The Greek's reading makes Agur humble about himself but confident about what God has taught him.

p: The Greek has "the name of his children". A later corrector of Codex Alexandrinus wrote "his son".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Jerome's Latin (filii eius)
readings.en: and what is the name of his son

readings.orig: ἢ τί ὄνομα τοῖς τέκνοις αὐτοῦ
readings.en: or what is the name of his children

why: The Hebrew singular is the harder and better-supported reading, and the Latin agrees. The Greek plural may reflect a translator who thought of God's heavenly "sons" or of Israel's people. Swete's notes report that a later hand in Codex Alexandrinus changed it to "his son" (τῷ υἱῷ).

t: "Who is the LORD?" or "Who sees me?"
p: In the Greek the full man says, "Who sees me?", denying not God but that God watches.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Jerome's Latin
readings.en: Who is YHWH?
Who sees me?

why: The Hebrew is the base text. The Greek translator avoided having a speaker in Scripture say "Who is the LORD?", or he interpreted it: the sated person's denial is practical, the belief that God does not see (compare Psalm 10:11). The Greek also adds that the full man "becomes a liar".

a: Do not run down a servant to his master
p: The Greek reads, "Do not hand a servant over to a master", like Deuteronomy's law about runaway slaves.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (Qere "his masters", a plural of majesty; Ketiv "his master")
readings.en: do not slander a servant to his master
readings.plain: Do not run down a servant to his master

readings.orig: μὴ παραδῷς οἰκέτην εἰς χεῖρας δεσπότου
readings.en: do not hand a household servant over into a master's hands
readings.plain: Do not hand a servant over to a master

why: The Hebrew verb is "slander", which fits the curse that follows. The Greek seems to have read the verse in the light of Deuteronomy 23:15. The Ketiv and Qere differ only in singular and plural, with the same meaning.

t: The barren womb, or a woman's passion?
p: The Greek has "Hades and a woman's passion and Tartarus", making the womb into desire.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Jerome's Latin (os vulvae)
readings.en: and the closing of the womb
and a woman's passion, and Tartarus

why: The Hebrew fits the list of things that cannot be filled. The Greek turned the image into sexual desire, and added Tartarus, the Greek name for the deepest underworld, perhaps as a second rendering of Sheol.

p: The Greek has "the old age of a mother", from a different reading of a rare Hebrew word.

readings.en: the obedience of a mother (obedience owed to her)
dishonoring a mother's old age

why: Yiqqahat appears only here and in Genesis 49:10 ("obedience"). The Greek, and some modern scholars, read a word for old age (compare 23:22, "Do not look down on your mother because she has grown old"). The Hebrew is the harder reading and is followed.

t: "With a young woman" or "in his youth"?
p: The Greek reads "the ways of a man in youth", not "with a young woman".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Jerome's Latin (in adulescentula, "in a young girl")
readings.en: with (literally 'in') a young woman
the ways of a man in youth

why: The Hebrew has the noun 'almah, and the Latin agrees. The Greek probably read the same letters as a word for youth ('alumim) or chose a modest rendering. The Hebrew fits 30:20, which turns to a woman.

a: The words of Lemuel, a king: the oracle with which his mother disciplined him.
t: "A king: the oracle" or "king of Massa"?
p: Read with the Hebrew accents, massa' is "oracle". Read without them, Lemuel is "king of Massa".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), following its accents, which divide after "king"; KJV
readings.orig: דִּבְרֵי לְמוּאֵל מֶלֶךְ מַשָּׂא אֲשֶׁר־יִסְּרַתּוּ אִמּוֹ
readings.en: The words of Lemuel, a king; an oracle that his mother taught him
readings.plain: The words of Lemuel, a king: the oracle with which his mother disciplined him.

readings.w: Same Hebrew words, read as one phrase; many modern scholars and some modern versions
readings.en: Lemuel, king of Massa
readings.plain: The words of Lemuel king of Massa, with which his mother disciplined him.

readings.orig: Οἱ ἐμοὶ λόγοι εἴρηνται ὑπὸ θεοῦ βασιλέως χρηματισμός ὃν ἐπαίδευσεν ἡ μήτηρ αὐτοῦ
readings.en: My words have been spoken by God, a king's oracle, which his mother taught
readings.plain: My words have been spoken by God, a king's oracle, which his mother taught him.

why: The accents of the Hebrew text put the pause after "king", so "oracle" goes with what follows. But "king" without "of" anything is unusual in a heading, and Massa is a known Arab people (Genesis 25:14). The Plain English Translation keeps the Masoretic division; the Massa reading is strong, and it would make both Agur (30:1) and Lemuel Arabian sages.
b: The Greek translator read Lemu'el as "by God" (lemo 'el, "to God") and so made the whole verse a claim of divine origin. The word chrēmatismos, "oracle, divine answer", shows that he understood massa' as "oracle". Jerome's Latin has "The words of King Lamuel; the vision with which his mother taught him".

p: The written Hebrew has "or"; the reading tradition says "where?". Some read "craving".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), Qere (the word as read aloud): אֵי, "where?"
readings.en: and for rulers, 'Where is beer?'

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), Ketiv (the word as written): אוֹ, "or"
readings.en: and for rulers, or beer

why: Both forms are in the Hebrew text itself. The Qere gives a vivid picture of a ruler calling for drink, and the Plain English Translation follows it. The Ketiv "or" is awkward but gives a simple sense ("or for rulers, beer"). Many modern scholars repoint the word as 'avvê, "desire for", which is why some versions say "crave". The Greek rewrites the verse.

p: Shanim is "scarlet". Read as shenayim, "double", the household wears two layers against the snow.

readings.en: is clothed in scarlet (cloth)

readings.w: Jerome's Latin (vestiti duplicibus); the same idea appears in the Septuagint's "double cloaks" in 31:22
readings.orig: omnes enim domestici eius vestiti duplicibus
readings.en: for all her household are clothed with double garments

why: The Hebrew letters can be read either way. "Double" makes better sense against snow, which is why Jerome and many scholars prefer it. But scarlet wool was costly and warm, and fine colored cloth fits 31:22. The Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic vowels.
b: The Greek of 31:21 is quite different: "Her husband takes no thought for those at home when he stays away anywhere, for all who are with her are clothed." Its next verse begins, "She made double cloaks for her husband."

a: A woman who fears the LORD, she is the one to be praised.
t: "A woman who fears the LORD" or "a wise woman"?
p: The Greek praises "a wise woman" and tells her to praise the fear of the Lord.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Jerome's Latin (mulier timens Dominum ipsa laudabitur)
readings.en: a woman who fears YHWH, she will be praised
readings.plain: A woman who fears the LORD, she is the one to be praised.

readings.orig: γυνὴ γὰρ συνετὴ εὐλογεῖται, φόβον δὲ κυρίου αὕτη αἰνείτω
readings.en: for a wise woman is blessed, and let her praise the fear of the Lord
readings.plain: For a wise woman is blessed, and let her praise the fear of the Lord.

why: The Hebrew is the base text and fits the book's frame (1:7). The Greek splits the line into two thoughts and makes the woman the one who praises.

p: The Greek ends the book with "let her husband be praised at the gates".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Jerome's Latin (laudent eam in portis opera eius)
readings.en: and let her works praise her in the gates

readings.orig: καὶ αἰνείσθω ἐν πύλαις ὁ ἀνὴρ αὐτῆς
readings.en: and let her husband be praised in the gates

why: The Hebrew gives the last word to her own deeds, matching "the fruit of her hands" in the first line. The Greek moves the praise to her husband, as in 31:23. Codex Vaticanus also has "the fruit of her lips" for "hands" in the first line, where Rahlfs prints "hands".
